But we shall speak more exactly about these when our discourse arrives in order at the treatment of the aids to <term>induction</term> <gloss>logical method of inference</gloss>.

XLIII. Among the prerogatives of instances, we shall place in the twentieth position the dissecting instances; which we have also been accustomed to call *vindicating* <note>original: "vellicantes," literally "plucking" or "twitching," signifying instances that prick or stimulate the mind</note> instances, but for a different reason. We call them *vindicating* because they pluck at the intellect; we call them *dissecting* because they dissect nature, for which reason we sometimes name them the instances of Democritus. These are the ones that warn the intellect of the admirable and exquisite subtlety of nature, so that it may be roused and awakened to due attention, observation, and inquiry. For example: that a small drop of ink can be extended to so many letters or lines; that silver gilded only on the outside can be drawn out to such a length of gilded wire; that a tiny little worm, such as is found in the skin, possesses within itself a spirit and at the same time a configuration of dissimilar parts; that a small amount of saffron can color a whole cask of water; that a small amount of civet or perfume can scent a far greater volume of air; that a minute

<summary>Bacon introduces the twentieth prerogative of instances, termed dissecting or vindicating, which serve to sharpen the intellect by revealing the extreme subtlety of natural processes.</summary>
